claim: The hippocampus plays a critical role in processing information about temporal context.
source: The hippocampus is known to play a critical role in processing information about temporal context.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract without specific data from this study.

claim: Odor sequence processing epochs were characterized by distinct spectral profiles compared to track running epochs.
source: We found that odor sequence processing epochs were characterized by distinct spectral profiles and proximodistal CA1 gradients of theta and 20–40 Hz power than track running epochs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing spectral profiles between behavioral states.

claim: Odor sequence processing epochs showed proximodistal CA1 gradients of theta power that differed from track running epochs.
source: We found that odor sequence processing epochs were characterized by distinct spectral profiles and proximodistal CA1 gradients of theta and 20–40 Hz power than track running epochs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements of theta power across CA1 sites during different behavioral states.

claim: Odor sequence processing epochs showed proximodistal CA1 gradients of 20–40 Hz power that differed from track running epochs.
source: We found that odor sequence processing epochs were characterized by distinct spectral profiles and proximodistal CA1 gradients of theta and 20–40 Hz power than track running epochs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements of 20-40 Hz power across CA1 sites during different behavioral states.

claim: 20–40 Hz power was predictive of sequence memory performance.
source: We also discovered that 20–40 Hz power was predictive of sequence memory performance, particularly in proximal CA1 and during the plateau of high power observed in trials in which animals had to maintain their decision until instructed to respond.
evidence: This claim is supported by classification analyses showing that 20-40 Hz power predicts trial accuracy.

claim: 20–40 Hz power was particularly predictive of sequence memory performance in proximal CA1.
source: We also discovered that 20–40 Hz power was predictive of sequence memory performance, particularly in proximal CA1 and during the plateau of high power observed in trials in which animals had to maintain their decision until instructed to respond.
evidence: This claim is supported by feature selection analyses identifying proximal CA1 sites as most predictive.

claim: 20–40 Hz power was particularly predictive of sequence memory performance during the plateau of high power observed in trials in which animals had to maintain their decision until instructed to respond.
source: We also discovered that 20–40 Hz power was predictive of sequence memory performance, particularly in proximal CA1 and during the plateau of high power observed in trials in which animals had to maintain their decision until instructed to respond.
evidence: This claim is supported by analyses showing that steady-state power during hold-response trials predicts accuracy.

claim: Dynamics of 20–40 Hz power along the CA1 axis are linked to trial-specific processing of nonspatial information critical to order judgments.
source: Altogether, these results provide evidence that dynamics of 20–40 Hz power along the CA1 axis are linked to trial-specific processing of nonspatial information critical to order judgments and are consistent with a role for 20–40 Hz power in gating information processing.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the experimental findings regarding 20-40 Hz power and task performance.

claim: 20–40 Hz power dynamics are consistent with a role in gating information processing.
source: Altogether, these results provide evidence that dynamics of 20–40 Hz power along the CA1 axis are linked to trial-specific processing of nonspatial information critical to order judgments and are consistent with a role for 20–40 Hz power in gating information processing.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation based on the observed power dynamics and comparison with literature on beta function.

claim: The hippocampus is critical for spatial learning and memory.
source: For instance, it is well established that the hippocampus is critical for spatial learning and memory (O'Keefe and Nadel, 1978) and that distinct oscillatory states are observed in hippocampal subregion CA1 during spatial navigation in rodents (see Colgin, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: Distinct oscillatory states are observed in hippocampal subregion CA1 during spatial navigation in rodents.
source: For instance, it is well established that the hippocampus is critical for spatial learning and memory (O'Keefe and Nadel, 1978) and that distinct oscillatory states are observed in hippocampal subregion CA1 during spatial navigation in rodents (see Colgin, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to review literature.

claim: CA1 theta power is prominent during spatial exploration.
source: CA1 theta power is prominent during spatial exploration, increases with running speed, and its phase is thought to link representations of spatial locations within a trajectory (Buzsáki and Moser, 2013; Drieu and Zugaro, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: CA1 theta power increases with running speed.
source: CA1 theta power is prominent during spatial exploration, increases with running speed, and its phase is thought to link representations of spatial locations within a trajectory (Buzsáki and Moser, 2013; Drieu and Zugaro, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Theta phase is thought to link representations of spatial locations within a trajectory.
source: CA1 theta power is prominent during spatial exploration, increases with running speed, and its phase is thought to link representations of spatial locations within a trajectory (Buzsáki and Moser, 2013; Drieu and Zugaro, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research and represents a theoretical interpretation.

claim: CA1 exhibits transient increases in slow gamma (25–55 Hz) power during exploration.
source: CA1 also exhibits transient increases in slow (25–55 Hz) and fast gamma (60–100 Hz) power during exploration, which are thought to be associated with retrieval and encoding processes, respectively (Colgin et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: CA1 exhibits transient increases in fast gamma (60–100 Hz) power during exploration.
source: CA1 also exhibits transient increases in slow (25–55 Hz) and fast gamma (60–100 Hz) power during exploration, which are thought to be associated with retrieval and encoding processes, respectively (Colgin et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Slow gamma (25–55 Hz) is thought to be associated with retrieval processes.
source: CA1 also exhibits transient increases in slow (25–55 Hz) and fast gamma (60–100 Hz) power during exploration, which are thought to be associated with retrieval and encoding processes, respectively (Colgin et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research and represents a theoretical interpretation.

claim: Fast gamma (60–100 Hz) is thought to be associated with encoding processes.
source: CA1 also exhibits transient increases in slow (25–55 Hz) and fast gamma (60–100 Hz) power during exploration, which are thought to be associated with retrieval and encoding processes, respectively (Colgin et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research and represents a theoretical interpretation.

claim: The hippocampus plays a key role in the processing of temporal information.
source: In addition to spatial information, accumulating evidence indicates that the hippocampus plays a key role in the processing of temporal information.
evidence: This claim is stated as accumulating evidence from the literature.

claim: The hippocampus is critical for remembering sequences of nonspatial events.
source: Consistent with its unique architecture and connectivity (McNaughton and Morris, 1987; Lisman, 1999; Foster and Knierim, 2012; Buzsáki and Tingley, 2018), a growing literature shows that the hippocampus is critical for remembering sequences of nonspatial events (Fortin et al., 2002; Kesner et al., 2002; Allen and Fortin, 2013; Eichenbaum, 2014) and hippocampal neurons code for temporal relationships among such events (MacDonald et al., 2011; Allen et al., 2016; Shahbaba et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Hippocampal neurons code for temporal relationships among nonspatial events.
source: Consistent with its unique architecture and connectivity (McNaughton and Morris, 1987; Lisman, 1999; Foster and Knierim, 2012; Buzsáki and Tingley, 2018), a growing literature shows that the hippocampus is critical for remembering sequences of nonspatial events (Fortin et al., 2002; Kesner et al., 2002; Allen and Fortin, 2013; Eichenbaum, 2014) and hippocampal neurons code for temporal relationships among such events (MacDonald et al., 2011; Allen et al., 2016; Shahbaba et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: ~4–8 Hz oscillations are observed in CA1 during tasks using olfactory stimuli.
source: Previous studies have observed theta oscillations in CA1 while rodents sampled task-relevant nonspatial stimuli, though the frequency range tended to be lower than during running. For example, ~4–8 Hz oscillations are observed in tasks using olfactory stimuli (Martin et al., 2007; Igarashi et al., 2014; Allen et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The hippocampus exhibits oscillations in the 20–40 Hz range during the processing of odor information.
source: In addition, the hippocampus exhibits oscillations in the 20–40 Hz range during the processing of odor information (Martin et al., 2007; Kay, 2014; Igarashi et al., 2014; Allen et al., 2016), with this signal varying in power across the proximodistal axis of CA1 (higher power in distal than proximal CA1; Igarashi et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: 20–40 Hz signal varies in power across the proximodistal axis of CA1, with higher power in distal than proximal CA1 during odor processing.
source: In addition, the hippocampus exhibits oscillations in the 20–40 Hz range during the processing of odor information (Martin et al., 2007; Kay, 2014; Igarashi et al., 2014; Allen et al., 2016), with this signal varying in power across the proximodistal axis of CA1 (higher power in distal than proximal CA1; Igarashi et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research by Igarashi et al., 2014.

claim: Beta has been hypothesized to serve a 'gating' function and reflects a 'status quo' signal bridging the period between a decision and a response.
source: Based on findings from striatal and cortical circuits (Leventhal et al., 2012; Engel and Fries, 2010; Schmidt et al., 2019), beta has been hypothesized to serve a 'gating' function and reflects a 'status quo' signal bridging the period between a decision and a response.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on beta function in other brain regions.

claim: Power in the 20–40 Hz and low-theta frequency ranges increased during the odor sequence processing periods.
source: As in our previous work (Allen et al., 2016), we report power increases in the 20–40 Hz and low-theta frequency ranges during the odor sequence processing periods.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the current study and reference to prior work.

claim: The same electrodes exhibited distinct spectral content during running on the track, characterized by high-theta power and a broadband increase in power for frequencies above 24 Hz.
source: Here, we extend these results by demonstrating that the same electrodes exhibited distinct spectral content in a different state (running on the track), which was characterized by high-theta power and a broadband increase in power for frequencies above 24 Hz.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing spectral profiles during different behavioral states.

claim: Power in the recruited frequencies varied along the proximodistal axis of CA1 in a behavioral state-dependent manner.
source: Notably, power in the recruited frequencies varied along the proximodistal axis of CA1 in a behavioral state-dependent manner.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing different gradients during odor processing vs. running.

claim: During odor processing, 20–40 Hz power was higher in proximal CA1.
source: During odor processing, 20–40 Hz power was higher in proximal CA1, whereas theta was higher in distal CA1.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements across CA1 sites during odor processing.

claim: During odor processing, theta was higher in distal CA1.
source: During odor processing, 20–40 Hz power was higher in proximal CA1, whereas theta was higher in distal CA1.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements across CA1 sites during odor processing.

claim: During running periods, theta was higher in proximal CA1.
source: During running periods, theta was higher in proximal, whereas >24 Hz power was higher in distal CA1.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements across CA1 sites during running.

claim: During running periods, >24 Hz power was higher in distal CA1.
source: During running periods, theta was higher in proximal, whereas >24 Hz power was higher in distal CA1.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements across CA1 sites during running.

claim: Power in the 20–40 Hz range increased with session performance.
source: Power in the 20–40 Hz range increased with session performance, whereas power in other frequency ranges did not.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing power across sessions with different performance levels.

claim: Power in other frequency ranges did not increase with session performance.
source: Power in the 20–40 Hz range increased with session performance, whereas power in other frequency ranges did not.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing different patterns for theta and gamma bands.

claim: The performance effect of 20-40 Hz power was primarily driven by activity on trials involving a sustained hold response.
source: This performance effect was primarily driven by activity on trials involving a sustained hold response.
evidence: This claim is supported by analyses showing performance effects selective to hold-response trials.

claim: 20–40 Hz power gradually increased during odor presentations on hold-response trials.
source: More specifically, we found that 20–40 Hz power gradually increased during odor presentations and reached a plateau (steady state) on these 'hold-response' trials, and that this steady-state power in the proximal segment of CA1 was key to predicting trial accuracy.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing power dynamics over time during trials.

claim: 20–40 Hz power reached a plateau (steady state) on hold-response trials.
source: More specifically, we found that 20–40 Hz power gradually increased during odor presentations and reached a plateau (steady state) on these 'hold-response' trials, and that this steady-state power in the proximal segment of CA1 was key to predicting trial accuracy.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing power dynamics over time during trials.

claim: Steady-state 20-40 Hz power in the proximal segment of CA1 was key to predicting trial accuracy.
source: More specifically, we found that 20–40 Hz power gradually increased during odor presentations and reached a plateau (steady state) on these 'hold-response' trials, and that this steady-state power in the proximal segment of CA1 was key to predicting trial accuracy.
evidence: This claim is supported by classification analyses showing that steady-state power in proximal CA1 predicts accuracy.

claim: 20–40 Hz power dynamics in the proximal segment of CA1 reflect a post-decision state that may serve to protect local, task-critical information processing from disruption and interference until a response can be performed.
source: Collectively, these results suggest that 20–40 Hz power dynamics in the proximal segment of CA1 are linked to processing the temporal context of nonspatial events and reflect a post-decision state that may serve to protect local, task-critical information processing from disruption and interference until a response can be performed.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the experimental findings based on the timing and characteristics of 20-40 Hz dynamics.

claim: Five rats were trained on an odor-based sequence memory task that critically depends on the hippocampus.
source: Five rats were trained on an odor-based sequence memory task that critically depends on the hippocampus (Fortin et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research showing hippocampal dependence of the task.

claim: Mean z-score 20–40 Hz power during 110–1200 ms period of odor presentation significantly increased toward proximal CA1.
source: Mean z-score 20–40 Hz power during 110–1200 ms period of odor presentation significantly increased toward proximal CA1 (significant effect of electrode: F3,2214 = 41.995, p<0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Mean z-score theta (4–12 Hz) power during 110–1200 ms period of odor presentation increased toward distal CA1.
source: Same as in (C), but for theta (4–12 Hz) showing increased power in the opposite direction (toward distal CA1; significant effect of electrode: F3,2214 = 60.952, p<0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Mean z-score higher frequency power during running (>24 Hz) increases toward distal CA1.
source: Mean z-score higher frequency power during running (>24 Hz to avoid theta's first harmonic) increases toward distal CA1 (significant effect of electrode: F3,2768 = 181.34, p<0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Mean z-score theta power during running increased toward proximal CA1.
source: Same as in (E), but for theta showing increased power in the opposite direction (toward proximal CA1; significant effect of electrode: F3,2768 = 71.005, p<0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Power in the most proximal site (electrode 1) showed significantly higher 20-40 Hz power compared to the two most distal sites (electrodes 3 and 4) during odor sampling.
source: Power in the most proximal site (electrode 1) showed significantly higher power compared to the two most distal sites (electrodes 3 and 4) (t2214 = –8.072, p<0.001 and t2214 = –8.024, p<0.001, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparisons of experimental data.

claim: Theta power during odor sampling in electrodes 2–4 was significantly higher compared to electrode 1.
source: Electrodes 2–4 showed significantly higher theta power compared to electrode 1 (t2214 = 5.008, p<0.001, t2214 = 11.99, p<0.001, and t2214 = 10.733, p<0.001, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparisons of experimental data.

claim: The 20–40 Hz power observed during odor sampling was weak during running.
source: More specifically, the 20–40 Hz power observed during odor sampling was weak during running.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of spectral profiles between behavioral states.

claim: Theta power during running was significantly higher in proximal CA1.
source: Additionally, contrary to the odor processing periods, theta power during running was significantly higher in proximal CA1 (LMEM ANOVA significant effect of electrode: F3,2768 = 71.005, p<0.001; Figure 2F) and was characterized by a higher center frequency (~9 Hz during running compared to ~6 Hz during odor sampling).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Theta during running was characterized by a higher center frequency (~9 Hz) compared to during odor sampling (~6 Hz).
source: Additionally, contrary to the odor processing periods, theta power during running was significantly higher in proximal CA1 (LMEM ANOVA significant effect of electrode: F3,2768 = 71.005, p<0.001; Figure 2F) and was characterized by a higher center frequency (~9 Hz during running compared to ~6 Hz during odor sampling).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of spectral characteristics during different behavioral states.

claim: The running period was characterized by increased high-frequency broadband power (>24 Hz), which significantly increased toward distal CA1.
source: The running period was also characterized by increased high-frequency broadband power (>24 Hz to avoid theta's first harmonic), which significantly increased toward distal CA1 (LMEM ANOVA significant effect of electrode: F3,2768 = 181.34, p<0.001; Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: 20–40 Hz power significantly increased with performance level.
source: We found that 20–40 Hz power significantly increased with performance level (LMEM ANOVA significant effect of session: F2,4812 = 46.71, p<0.001), which complements our previous study showing learning-related differences in waveform amplitude (Allen et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis comparing power across sessions with different performance levels.

claim: The well-trained session showed significantly higher 20-40 Hz power compared to novel 1 session.
source: When collapsing across electrodes, the well-trained session showed significantly higher power compared to novel 1 (t4812=8.451, p<0.001), while power during the novel 1 and novel 2 sessions did not significantly differ (t4812=1.470, p=0.14168).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparisons of experimental data.

claim: Power during the novel 1 and novel 2 sessions did not significantly differ.
source: When collapsing across electrodes, the well-trained session showed significantly higher power compared to novel 1 (t4812=8.451, p<0.001), while power during the novel 1 and novel 2 sessions did not significantly differ (t4812=1.470, p=0.14168).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparisons of experimental data.

claim: The performance effect of 20-40 Hz power did not significantly vary across the proximodistal axis.
source: Notably, this performance effect did not significantly vary across the proximodistal axis (nonsignificant interaction between electrode and session F6,4806 = 0.745, p=0.614), but instead scaled with the local amplitude of 20–40 Hz, suggesting that this behavioral correlate is present throughout dorsal CA1.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis showing no interaction effect.

claim: The performance effect of 20-40 Hz power scaled with the local amplitude of 20–40 Hz, suggesting that this behavioral correlate is present throughout dorsal CA1.
source: Notably, this performance effect did not significantly vary across the proximodistal axis (nonsignificant interaction between electrode and session F6,4806 = 0.745, p=0.614), but instead scaled with the local amplitude of 20–40 Hz, suggesting that this behavioral correlate is present throughout dorsal CA1.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the statistical findings regarding the performance effect.

claim: Average 20-40 Hz power was significantly higher in electrode 1 compared to electrodes 2–4.
source: More precisely, average power was significantly higher in electrode 1 compared to electrodes 2–4 (t4812 = –2.969, p=0.003, t4812 = –8.896, p<0.001, and t4812 = –11.095, p<0.001, respectively) (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparisons of experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Theta power decreased with session performance.
source: Whereas 20–40 Hz power increased with performance, theta and fast gamma power decreased (theta LMEM ANOVA: F2,4806 = 7.681, p<0.001; fast gamma LMEM ANOVA: F2,4806 = 8.147, p<0.001) and slow gamma showed a nonlinear relationship with session performance (LMEM ANOVA: F2,4815 = 5.993, p=0.003).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Fast gamma power decreased with session performance.
source: Whereas 20–40 Hz power increased with performance, theta and fast gamma power decreased (theta LMEM ANOVA: F2,4806 = 7.681, p<0.001; fast gamma LMEM ANOVA: F2,4806 = 8.147, p<0.001) and slow gamma showed a nonlinear relationship with session performance (LMEM ANOVA: F2,4815 = 5.993, p=0.003).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Slow gamma showed a nonlinear relationship with session performance.
source: Whereas 20–40 Hz power increased with performance, theta and fast gamma power decreased (theta LMEM ANOVA: F2,4806 = 7.681, p<0.001; fast gamma LMEM ANOVA: F2,4806 = 8.147, p<0.001) and slow gamma showed a nonlinear relationship with session performance (LMEM ANOVA: F2,4815 = 5.993, p=0.003).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The 20–40 Hz band is unique in showing a distinctive increase in power with performance level.
source: This suggests that the 20–40 Hz band is unique in showing a distinctive increase in power with performance level.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation based on comparison of performance effects across frequency bands.

claim: The rising phase (~0–750 ms) of 20-40 Hz power was similar across trial types.
source: Aligning data to port entry (Figure 4A, left), we observed that the rising phase (~0–750 ms) was similar across trial types and that differences emerged later in the trial.
evidence: This claim is supported by visual inspection and analysis of power dynamics shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Power was sustained (reaching steady-state) on trials in which animals performed a 'hold' response (InSeq+ and OutSeq-).
source: Specifically, we observed that power was sustained (reaching steady-state) on trials in which animals performed a 'hold'response (InSeq+ and OutSeq-), whereas it fell off earlier (during the transient phase) on trials in which the animals performed a 'withdraw' response (OutSeq+ and InSeq-).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of power dynamics across trial types.

claim: 20-40 Hz power fell off earlier (during the transient phase) on trials in which the animals performed a 'withdraw' response (OutSeq+ and InSeq-).
source: Specifically, we observed that power was sustained (reaching steady-state) on trials in which animals performed a 'hold'response (InSeq+ and OutSeq-), whereas it fell off earlier (during the transient phase) on trials in which the animals performed a 'withdraw' response (OutSeq+ and InSeq-).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of power dynamics across trial types.

claim: The withdrawal response occurs during steady-state for the hold responses.
source: Aligning data to port withdrawal confirmed that the withdrawal response occurs during steady-state for the hold responses, but stochastically during the transient response or early steady-state for the withdraw responses (Figure 4A, right).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of power dynamics aligned to port withdrawal shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The withdrawal response occurs stochastically during the transient response or early steady-state for the withdraw responses.
source: Aligning data to port withdrawal confirmed that the withdrawal response occurs during steady-state for the hold responses, but stochastically during the transient response or early steady-state for the withdraw responses (Figure 4A, right).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of power dynamics aligned to port withdrawal shown in Figure 4A.

claim: There were no significant differences between trial types in 20-40 Hz power during the 250–500 ms epoch relative to port entry.
source: There were no significant differences between trial types in this epoch (LMEM ANOVA nonsignificant effect of trial type: F3,749 = 0.480, p=0.6935; Figure 4C, left), suggesting that the 20–40 Hz transient phase did not differ with response type (hold/withdraw) nor accuracy (correct/incorrect).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The 20–40 Hz transient phase did not differ with response type (hold/withdraw) nor accuracy (correct/incorrect).
source: There were no significant differences between trial types in this epoch (LMEM ANOVA nonsignificant effect of trial type: F3,749 = 0.480, p=0.6935; Figure 4C, left), suggesting that the 20–40 Hz transient phase did not differ with response type (hold/withdraw) nor accuracy (correct/incorrect).
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the statistical finding of no significant differences.

claim: There was a significant effect of trial type on 20-40 Hz power during the 250 ms period preceding port withdrawal.
source: Although there was a significant effect of trial type when focusing on power during the 250 ms period preceding port withdrawal (LMEM ANOVA: F3,743 = 9.451, p<0.001; Figure 4C, right), this effect appears primarily due to the post hoc observation mentioned above (as well as the variability observed on InSeq- trials).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: InSeq+ trials (hold responses) showed higher 20-40 Hz power than OutSeq+ and InSeq- (withdraw responses) trial types during the 250 ms period preceding port withdrawal.
source: In fact, InSeq+ trials (hold responses) were higher than OutSeq+ and InSeq- (withdraw responses) trial types (t743 = –2.829, p=0.005 and t743 = –4.787, p<0.001, respectively), but power in this epoch did not significantly differ between the hold-response trials (InSeq+ and OutSeq-) (t743 = –0.458, p=0.647).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparisons of experimental data.

claim: Power in the 250 ms period preceding port withdrawal did not significantly differ between the hold-response trials (InSeq+ and OutSeq-).
source: In fact, InSeq+ trials (hold responses) were higher than OutSeq+ and InSeq- (withdraw responses) trial types (t743 = –2.829, p=0.005 and t743 = –4.787, p<0.001, respectively), but power in this epoch did not significantly differ between the hold-response trials (InSeq+ and OutSeq-) (t743 = –0.458, p=0.647).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparisons of experimental data.

claim: A random forest classifier using 20-40 Hz power in the 650–1200 ms period relative to port entry in the three most proximal CA1 electrodes was sufficient to discriminate between correct and incorrect temporal order judgments (InSeq+ and OutSeq-).
source: We found that these three features were sufficient to discriminate between correct and incorrect temporal order judgments (InSeq+ and OutSeq-, respectively). In fact, the classifier performed with mean areas under the curve (AUC) of 0.588 and 0.477 on the observed and shuffled data, respectively (Figure 4D), and a Mann–Whitney U test showed a statistically significant difference between the observed and null AUC values (with higher classification performance on the observed data; U = 839,538, p<0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by classification analysis results shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The classifier performed with mean AUC of 0.588 on the observed data and 0.477 on shuffled data.
source: In fact, the classifier performed with mean areas under the curve (AUC) of 0.588 and 0.477 on the observed and shuffled data, respectively (Figure 4D), and a Mann–Whitney U test showed a statistically significant difference between the observed and null AUC values (with higher classification performance on the observed data; U = 839,538, p<0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by classification analysis results.

claim: There was a significant effect of trial type (InSeq+ vs. OutSeq-) on 20-40 Hz power during the 650–1200 ms epoch.
source: Post hoc group analyses of the identified feature (650–1200 ms epoch) showed a significant effect of trial type (InSeq+ vs. OutSeq-; LMEM ANOVA: F1,2406 = 32.687, p<0.001) and electrode (F3,2406 = 90.573, p<0.001), but no significant interaction (F3,2406 = 0.193, p=0.901) (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Power during the 650–1200 ms epoch was significantly higher on incorrect temporal order judgments (OutSeq- power was higher than InSeq+).
source: Interestingly, power was significantly higher on incorrect temporal order judgments (OutSeq- power was higher than InSeq+).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: 20–40 Hz steady-state power in proximal CA1 is predictive of accuracy for temporal order judgments during hold-response trials.
source: Altogether, these results demonstrate that 20–40 Hz steady-state power in proximal CA1 is predictive of accuracy for temporal order judgments during hold-response trials, and that incorrect judgments are associated with significantly higher 20–40 Hz power.
evidence: This claim is a summary of the classification and statistical analysis results.

claim: Incorrect temporal order judgments are associated with significantly higher 20–40 Hz power.
source: Altogether, these results demonstrate that 20–40 Hz steady-state power in proximal CA1 is predictive of accuracy for temporal order judgments during hold-response trials, and that incorrect judgments are associated with significantly higher 20–40 Hz power.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis showing higher power on OutSeq- trials.

claim: The session performance effect on 20-40 Hz power was observed for the hold-response trial types (InSeq+, OutSeq-).
source: This performance effect was observed for the hold-response trial types (InSeq+, OutSeq-; Figure 5A) but not the withdraw-response trial types (Figure 5B; which included OutSeq+ trials where order memory retrieval is presumably intact and improved with training).
evidence: This claim is supported by cluster-based permutation testing results shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The session performance effect on 20-40 Hz power was not observed for the withdraw-response trial types.
source: This performance effect was observed for the hold-response trial types (InSeq+, OutSeq-; Figure 5A) but not the withdraw-response trial types (Figure 5B; which included OutSeq+ trials where order memory retrieval is presumably intact and improved with training).
evidence: This claim is supported by cluster-based permutation testing results shown in Figure 5B.

claim: A significant effect of performance level was observed for both hold-response trial types (InSeq+ and OutSeq-) during the identified epoch.
source: During this epoch, a significant effect of performance level was observed for both hold-response trial types (InSeq+ and OutSeq-; LMEM ANOVA significant effect of performance: F2,1229 = 14.184, p<0.001 and F2,173 = 12.072, p<0.001, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: For both hold-response trial types, epoch power during the well-trained session was significantly higher than that of the novel 1 session.
source: For both trial types, epoch power during the well-trained session was significantly higher than that of the novel 1 session (t1229 = 3.984, p<0.001 and t173 = 4.462, p<0.001, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparisons of experimental data.

claim: Epoch power during both withdraw-response trial types (OutSeq+ and InSeq-) did not significantly differ with performance.
source: In contrast, epoch power during both withdraw-response trial types (OutSeq+ and InSeq-) did not significantly differ with performance (LMEM ANOVA nonsignificant effect of performance: F2,128 = 0.384, p=0.682 and F2,116 = 0.796, p=0.453, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Power increases with session performance may reflect a post-decision state that varies with knowledge of the sequence.
source: These results support the notion that power increases with session performance may reflect a post-decision state that varies with knowledge of the sequence.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the experimental findings regarding selective performance effects.

claim: Running and odor sequence processing epochs were characterized by different spectral features.
source: First, we demonstrated that running and odor sequence processing epochs were characterized by different spectral features.
evidence: This claim is a summary of experimental findings comparing spectral profiles.

claim: Running was associated with increased power in theta (4–12 Hz) and >24 Hz frequency ranges.
source: Running was associated with increased power in theta (4–12 Hz) and >24 Hz frequency ranges, whereas odor sequence processing was associated with increased power in theta (at a lower center frequency than during running) and 20–40 Hz ranges.
evidence: This claim is a summary of experimental findings regarding spectral profiles during running.

claim: Odor sequence processing was associated with increased power in theta (at a lower center frequency than during running) and 20–40 Hz ranges.
source: Running was associated with increased power in theta (4–12 Hz) and >24 Hz frequency ranges, whereas odor sequence processing was associated with increased power in theta (at a lower center frequency than during running) and 20–40 Hz ranges.
evidence: This claim is a summary of experimental findings regarding spectral profiles during odor processing.

claim: In both behavioral states there were distinct gradients of recruited frequency power along the CA1 proximodistal axis.
source: Second, we showed that in both behavioral states there were distinct gradients of recruited frequency power along the CA1 proximodistal axis.
evidence: This claim is a summary of experimental findings regarding spatial gradients.

claim: There were differential performance-related effects across frequency bands.
source: Third, we observed differential performance-related effects across frequency bands; 20–40 Hz power dynamics were positively associated with performance across sessions, while theta and fast gamma demonstrated a negative association.
evidence: This claim is a summary of experimental findings comparing performance effects across bands.

claim: 20–40 Hz power dynamics were positively associated with performance across sessions.
source: Third, we observed differential performance-related effects across frequency bands; 20–40 Hz power dynamics were positively associated with performance across sessions, while theta and fast gamma demonstrated a negative association.
evidence: This claim is a summary of experimental findings regarding 20-40 Hz performance effects.

claim: Theta and fast gamma demonstrated a negative association with performance across sessions.
source: Third, we observed differential performance-related effects across frequency bands; 20–40 Hz power dynamics were positively associated with performance across sessions, while theta and fast gamma demonstrated a negative association.
evidence: This claim is a summary of experimental findings regarding theta and fast gamma performance effects.

claim: Both hold-response trials (InSeq+ and OutSeq-) and withdraw-response trials (OutSeq+ and InSeq-) displayed a transient phase where 20–40 Hz power gradually increased at a similar rate.
source: Both hold-response trials (InSeq+ and OutSeq-) and withdraw-response trials (OutSeq+ and InSeq-) displayed a transient phase where 20–40 Hz power gradually increased at a similar rate.
evidence: This claim is a summary of experimental findings regarding power dynamics across trial types.

claim: 20–40 Hz power declined on withdraw-response (presumed OutSeq decisions) trials.
source: However, dynamics subsequently diverged; 20–40 Hz power declined on withdraw-response (presumed OutSeq decisions) trials while hold-response trials (presumed InSeq decisions) displayed a steady-state period of elevated 20–40 Hz power that remained until the animal withdrew.
evidence: This claim is a summary of experimental findings regarding power dynamics on withdraw-response trials.

claim: Hold-response trials (presumed InSeq decisions) displayed a steady-state period of elevated 20–40 Hz power that remained until the animal withdrew.
source: However, dynamics subsequently diverged; 20–40 Hz power declined on withdraw-response (presumed OutSeq decisions) trials while hold-response trials (presumed InSeq decisions) displayed a steady-state period of elevated 20–40 Hz power that remained until the animal withdrew.
evidence: This claim is a summary of experimental findings regarding power dynamics on hold-response trials.

claim: The steady phase of 20–40 Hz power in proximal CA1 is a key component carrying task-critical information.
source: Fifth, we identified the steady phase of 20–40 Hz power in proximal CA1 as a key component carrying task-critical information.
evidence: This claim is a summary of experimental findings from classification analyses.

claim: The steady phase component of 20-40 Hz power (observed on hold-response trials) increased with session performance.
source: In fact, this component of the signal (observed on hold-response trials) increased with session performance and was predictive of the accuracy of temporal order judgments.
evidence: This claim is a summary of experimental findings regarding the steady phase.

claim: The steady phase component of 20-40 Hz power was predictive of the accuracy of temporal order judgments.
source: In fact, this component of the signal (observed on hold-response trials) increased with session performance and was predictive of the accuracy of temporal order judgments.
evidence: This claim is a summary of experimental findings from classification analyses.

claim: Evidence for functional heterogeneity along the CA1 proximodistal axis has been previously reported.
source: Evidence for functional heterogeneity along the CA1 proximodistal axis has been previously reported (Henriksen et al., 2010; Hartzell et al., 2013; Nakazawa et al., 2016; Ng et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Proximal and distal CA1 are more anatomically and functionally associated with MEC and LEC, respectively.
source: Such heterogeneity is not surprising given the known connectivity gradients of the lateral and medial entorhinal cortices (LEC and MEC; van Strien et al., 2009; Witter et al., 2017), namely, that proximal and distal CA1 are more anatomically and functionally associated with MEC and LEC, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on connectivity.

claim: Igarashi et al., 2014 showed that 20–40 Hz power and LEC-CA1 coherence were higher in distal CA1 during performance of an odor-place association task.
source: For instance, Igarashi et al., 2014 showed that 20–40 Hz power and LEC-CA1 coherence were higher in distal CA1 during performance of an odor-place association task (whereas here we show higher power in proximal CA1).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The power increase in distal CA1 observed by Igarashi et al. may reflect a stronger engagement of the LEC-dCA1 component of the circuit.
source: Since performance in their task depends on the correct identification of the specific perceptual features that distinguish one odor from another, the power increase in distal CA1 may reflect a stronger engagement of the LEC-dCA1 component of the circuit (as LEC receives strong olfactory input, including direct projections from the olfactory bulb; Haberly and Price, 1978; Agster and Burwell, 2009).
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of prior findings based on task demands and connectivity.

claim: LEC receives strong olfactory input, including direct projections from the olfactory bulb.
source: Since performance in their task depends on the correct identification of the specific perceptual features that distinguish one odor from another, the power increase in distal CA1 may reflect a stronger engagement of the LEC-dCA1 component of the circuit (as LEC receives strong olfactory input, including direct projections from the olfactory bulb; Haberly and Price, 1978; Agster and Burwell, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on anatomy.

claim: The power increase in proximal CA1 observed in this study may reflect preferential engagement of the MEC-pCA1 component of the circuit due to temporal requirements.
source: In contrast, in our experiment, identification of the presented odor alone is insufficient for correct performance – the animal must further identify whether the odor is being presented in the appropriate temporal context. The power increase in proximal CA1 we observed may reflect the fact that this additional temporal requirement preferentially engaged the MEC-pCA1 component of the circuit.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the experimental findings based on task demands.

claim: Optogenetic inactivation of MEC disrupted temporal coding in CA1, while sparing spatial and object coding.
source: Interestingly, although MEC is typically associated with spatial navigation functions, this interpretation is supported by a recent study by Robinson et al., 2017, in which they demonstrated that optogenetic inactivation of MEC disrupted temporal coding in CA1, while sparing spatial and object coding.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The MEC→proximal CA1 microcircuit may be important for the processing of nonspatial temporal information.
source: Together with the proximodistal pattern we observed, these results suggest that perhaps the MEC→proximal CA1 microcircuit may be important for the processing of nonspatial temporal information.
evidence: This claim is a speculative interpretation based on the current findings and prior research.

claim: Beta serves a gating function that helps lock in and protect a neural state representing trial-critical information.
source: Of particular interest here is the hypothesis that beta serves a gating function that helps lock in and protect a neural state representing trial-critical information (i.e., maintain the status quo; Engel and Fries, 2010; Weiss and Mueller, 2012).
evidence: This claim is a hypothesis from prior research cited in the manuscript.

claim: Beta power is attenuated during encoding.
source: This is in line with observations that beta power is attenuated during encoding (Lundqvist et al., 2016; Zavala et al., 2017) and complements findings that transcranial magnetic stimulation at the beta frequency impairs encoding (Hanslmayr et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Transcranial magnetic stimulation at the beta frequency impairs encoding.
source: This is in line with observations that beta power is attenuated during encoding (Lundqvist et al., 2016; Zavala et al., 2017) and complements findings that transcranial magnetic stimulation at the beta frequency impairs encoding (Hanslmayr et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The steady-state 20–40 Hz period observed on hold-response trials reflects the system actively maintaining an ensemble or network state in support of the decision to perform a hold response.
source: The perspective that beta helps maintain the status quo would predict that the steady-state 20–40 Hz period observed on hold-response trials reflects the system actively maintaining an ensemble or network state in support of the decision to perform a hold response.
evidence: This claim is a theoretical interpretation based on the beta gating hypothesis.

claim: Specific odor and temporal context information is represented at the single-cell and ensemble levels during the late trial period.
source: Though it is possible the post-decision ensemble state reflects a general signal, such as a postural one or a nonspecific signal of a temporal context match, our current finding showed that this epoch is predictive of accuracy and our previous work showed that specific odor and temporal context information is represented at the single-cell (Allen et al., 2016) and ensemble (Shahbaba et al., 2022) levels during this late trial period.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work by the authors.

claim: What is 'locked in' during the steady-state 20–40 Hz period may be the trial-specific content supporting the animal's judgment that the odor is presented in the correct temporal context.
source: It is therefore possible that what is 'locked in' during the steady-state 20–40 Hz period is the trial-specific content supporting the animal's judgment that the odor is presented in the correct temporal context.
evidence: This claim is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: High beta during the well-trained session possibly reflects higher levels of gating and effective suppression of distracting processes.
source: High beta during the well-trained session possibly reflects higher levels of gating and effective suppression of distracting processes; this is a high-performing session in which the sequence is already well-learned, minimizing the need for additional knowledge acquisition.
evidence: This claim is a speculative interpretation of the performance-related effects.

claim: Lower beta power in the novel 1 and 2 sessions may enable flexible knowledge acquisition processes that would otherwise have been interrupted.
source: In contrast, lower beta power in the novel 1 and 2 sessions, which are associated with a higher demand for encoding, may enable flexible knowledge acquisition processes that would otherwise have been interrupted.
evidence: This claim is a speculative interpretation of the performance-related effects.

claim: There are complementary dynamics of beta and gamma rhythms.
source: Consistent with complementary dynamics of beta and gamma rhythms previously reported (Howe et al., 2011; Lundqvist et al., 2016), we find an inverse pattern for fast gamma power (and theta) with performance, whereby fast gamma power is higher during acquisition of a new sequence (novel 1–2) and decreases with session performance.
evidence: This claim is supported by the current findings and citations to prior research.

claim: Fast gamma power is higher during acquisition of a new sequence (novel 1–2) and decreases with session performance.
source: Consistent with complementary dynamics of beta and gamma rhythms previously reported (Howe et al., 2011; Lundqvist et al., 2016), we find an inverse pattern for fast gamma power (and theta) with performance, whereby fast gamma power is higher during acquisition of a new sequence (novel 1–2) and decreases with session performance.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: Proximal CA1 higher steady-state beta levels during incorrect trials may reflect over-suppression, leading to interference with processes needed for successful performance on the task.
source: Proximal CA1 higher steady-state beta levels during incorrect trials may reflect over-suppression, leading to interference with processes needed for successful performance on the task.
evidence: This claim is a speculative interpretation of the finding that OutSeq- trials have higher power.

claim: The appropriate level of suppression may be advantageous in attenuating distractions, but too high a level may impede essential processes.
source: In other words, the appropriate level of suppression may be advantageous in attenuating distractions, but too high a level may impede essential processes.
evidence: This claim is a theoretical interpretation of the relationship between beta power and performance.

claim: Increased beta in patients with Parkinson's disease is associated with highly sustained, rigid movements.
source: Consistent with this are clinical reports demonstrating that increased beta in patients with Parkinson's disease is associated with highly sustained, rigid movements (Chen et al., 2007; Pogosyan et al., 2009; Brown, 2007) and difficulty in switching behavioral paradigm (Stoffers et al., 2001); clinically disrupting beta power improves these symptoms, with a side effect of inability to ignore distractions and difficulty in focusing on the task at hand (Cools et al., 2003; Moustafa et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to clinical research.

claim: Increased beta in patients with Parkinson's disease is associated with difficulty in switching behavioral paradigm.
source: Consistent with this are clinical reports demonstrating that increased beta in patients with Parkinson's disease is associated with highly sustained, rigid movements (Chen et al., 2007; Pogosyan et al., 2009; Brown, 2007) and difficulty in switching behavioral paradigm (Stoffers et al., 2001); clinically disrupting beta power improves these symptoms, with a side effect of inability to ignore distractions and difficulty in focusing on the task at hand (Cools et al., 2003; Moustafa et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to clinical research.

claim: Clinically disrupting beta power improves Parkinson's symptoms, with a side effect of inability to ignore distractions and difficulty in focusing on the task at hand.
source: Consistent with this are clinical reports demonstrating that increased beta in patients with Parkinson's disease is associated with highly sustained, rigid movements (Chen et al., 2007; Pogosyan et al., 2009; Brown, 2007) and difficulty in switching behavioral paradigm (Stoffers et al., 2001); clinically disrupting beta power improves these symptoms, with a side effect of inability to ignore distractions and difficulty in focusing on the task at hand (Cools et al., 2003; Moustafa et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to clinical research.

claim: Higher steady-state power may represent a point of no return, despite retrieval of knowledge that suggests a change in behavior.
source: Alternatively, beta effects may reflect more of a threshold process: higher steady-state power may represent a point of no return, despite retrieval of knowledge that suggests a change in behavior.
evidence: This claim is an alternative speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: The likelihood of stopping decreased when a second cue occurred during the beta synchronization event elicited from the first cue, reflecting a 'closed gate' on the behavioral state initially cued.
source: This latter possibility is consistent with the observation made by Leventhal et al., 2012, in which animals were given a second stop cue following an initial go cue. The likelihood of stopping decreased when the second cue occurred during the beta synchronization event elicited from the first cue, reflecting a 'closed gate' on the behavioral state initially cued.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Utilization of a sensory cue to inform motor output has been shown to recruit ~20 Hz (beta) in cortico-basal ganglia circuits.
source: Utilization of a sensory cue to inform motor output has been shown to recruit ~20 Hz (beta) in cortico-basal ganglia circuits (CBG, Leventhal et al., 2012), CA1-striatal circuits (Lansink et al., 2016), and the dentate gyrus (DG; Rangel et al., 2015), giving rise to a working hypothesis for the functional role of ~20 Hz in sensorimotor integration.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Utilization of a sensory cue to inform motor output has been shown to recruit ~20 Hz (beta) in CA1-striatal circuits.
source: Utilization of a sensory cue to inform motor output has been shown to recruit ~20 Hz (beta) in cortico-basal ganglia circuits (CBG, Leventhal et al., 2012), CA1-striatal circuits (Lansink et al., 2016), and the dentate gyrus (DG; Rangel et al., 2015), giving rise to a working hypothesis for the functional role of ~20 Hz in sensorimotor integration.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Utilization of a sensory cue to inform motor output has been shown to recruit ~20 Hz (beta) in the dentate gyrus.
source: Utilization of a sensory cue to inform motor output has been shown to recruit ~20 Hz (beta) in cortico-basal ganglia circuits (CBG, Leventhal et al., 2012), CA1-striatal circuits (Lansink et al., 2016), and the dentate gyrus (DG; Rangel et al., 2015), giving rise to a working hypothesis for the functional role of ~20 Hz in sensorimotor integration.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: It is possible that sensorimotor integration contributed to the oscillations observed in this study.
source: Since, in this study, animals utilized the odor cue to either maintain or terminate a hold posture, it is possible that this aspect of sensorimotor integration contributed to the oscillations we observed.
evidence: This claim is a speculative interpretation acknowledging a potential confound.

claim: A proportion of CA1 neurons' spiking activity is phase-locked to 20–40 Hz oscillations.
source: Though we previously showed that the spiking activity of a proportion of CA1 neurons is phase-locked to these 20–40 Hz oscillations (Allen et al., 2016), we cannot rule out the possibility that volume conduction contributed to the presence of these rhythms and their gradients.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: A prior study performed current source density analysis for hippocampal 15–35 Hz power and localized this rhythm to the DG.
source: A prior study performed current source density analysis for hippocampal 15–35 Hz power, spanning DG, CA3, and CA1, and localized this rhythm to the DG (Rangel et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Coherence in the beta range between the hippocampus and olfactory regions has been previously reported during odor-dependent tasks.
source: As mentioned earlier, coherence in the beta range between the hippocampus and olfactory regions (Martin and Ravel, 2014; Kay, 2014), as well as with the entorhinal cortex (Igarashi et al., 2014), has been previously reported during odor-dependent tasks.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Coherence in the beta range between the hippocampus and entorhinal cortex has been previously reported during odor-dependent tasks.
source: As mentioned earlier, coherence in the beta range between the hippocampus and olfactory regions (Martin and Ravel, 2014; Kay, 2014), as well as with the entorhinal cortex (Igarashi et al., 2014), has been previously reported during odor-dependent tasks.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Beta dynamics are not restricted to olfactory processing.
source: Importantly, these dynamics are not restricted to olfactory processing (visual cues: Lansink et al., 2016; auditory cues: Leventhal et al., 2012) nor do they exclusively coordinate hippocampus with olfactory or medial temporal lobe regions.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research using different sensory modalities.

claim: Lansink et al., 2016 demonstrated CA1 beta (15–20 Hz) recruitment as rats responded in the presence of a reward-predictive visual cue that directed navigation.
source: Lansink et al., 2016 demonstrated CA1 beta (15–20 Hz) recruitment as rats responded in the presence of a reward-predictive visual cue that directed navigation (as opposed to goal-directed navigation absent a cue).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: During CA1 beta recruitment, neuronal firing was synchronized between CA1 and ventral striatum.
source: Notably, during this recruitment neuronal firing was synchronized between CA1 and ventral striatum (Lansink et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Prefrontal, perirhinal, and mid-thalamic regions have been shown to be critical for performance on the odor sequence task.
source: Specific to our task, structures connected to the hippocampus have also been shown to be critical for performance, including prefrontal, perirhinal, and mid-thalamic regions (Fortin et al., 2016; Jayachandran et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Beta may serve to bind brain regions together to coordinate distinct task-critical representations across regions and support goal-directed behavior.
source: As each structure likely contains region-specific representations, beta may serve to bind these regions together to coordinate these distinct task-critical representations across regions and support goal-directed behavior (Fries, 2005).
evidence: This claim is a theoretical interpretation supported by citation.

claim: Multiregional integration may serve as the general function of beta, which, in this paradigm, is in the service of supporting order memory judgments.
source: To clarify, multiregional integration may serve as the general function of beta, which, in our paradigm, is in the service of supporting order memory judgments.
evidence: This claim is a theoretical interpretation of beta function.

claim: Increases in CA1 beta have been reported in other task conditions and demands, such as exploration and novelty.
source: Increases in CA1 beta have been reported in other task conditions and demands, such as exploration and novelty (Berke et al., 2008; França et al., 2014), which could reflect multiregional integration supporting other forms of task-critical information processing.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Beta increases during exploration and novelty could reflect multiregional integration supporting other forms of task-critical information processing.
source: Increases in CA1 beta have been reported in other task conditions and demands, such as exploration and novelty (Berke et al., 2008; França et al., 2014), which could reflect multiregional integration supporting other forms of task-critical information processing.
evidence: This claim is a speculative interpretation of prior findings.
